stem: During a 2-month well-child visit, the nurse gives the birth parent a validated postpartum depression screening tool. Which explanation best describes why this screening is part of pediatric preventive care?

options.A: Repeated screening during early well-child visits creates opportunities to identify postpartum depression and connect the parent with further evaluation, treatment, and support that can benefit the parent-infant dyad.
options.B: A positive screening score allows the pediatric team to make a definitive psychiatric diagnosis without further clinical evaluation.
options.C: Screening is needed only when the infant has feeding, growth, or developmental problems that already suggest parental depression.
options.D: Once screening is completed at the 2-month visit, additional postpartum depression screening during later early-infancy well visits is unnecessary.

rationale: A is correct. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends routine postpartum depression screening of the birth parent with a validated tool at the infant's 1-, 2-, 4-, and 6-month well-child visits. Repeated screening provides multiple opportunities to identify depression, initiate support, and arrange referral or treatment when indicated; perinatal depression can affect the parent, infant, and parent-infant relationship. B is incorrect because a screening result identifies risk and the need for further evaluation rather than establishing a psychiatric diagnosis by itself. C is incorrect because AAP recommends routine screening at specified well-child visits rather than waiting for infant problems or overt parental symptoms. D is incorrect because AAP specifically recommends repeated screening through the 6-month well-child visit.
educational_objective: Explain that postpartum depression screening is a routine, repeated component of early well-child care because timely identification and referral can support the birth parent, infant, and parent-infant relationship; a positive screen requires further assessment rather than serving as a diagnosis by itself.
source_document_title: Incorporating Recognition and Management of Perinatal Depression Into Pediatric Practice; Preventive Care/Periodicity Schedule; Integrating Postpartum Depression Screening in Your Practice in 4 Steps
source_version_date: AAP Clinical Report 2019; AAP Preventive Care/Periodicity Schedule current page accessed 2026-08-17; AAP implementation guidance current page accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: AAP Clinical Report — Recommendations: routine PPD screening should be integrated into well-child visits at 1, 2, 4, and 6 months; screening should use a validated tool and positive findings should lead to intervention/referral. AAP Preventive Care/Periodicity Schedule — Maternal Depression Screening: screening at 1-, 2-, 4-, and 6-month visits. AAP implementation guidance — Screening: birth parent should be screened at the 1-, 2-, 4-, and 6-month well-infant visits using a validated tool.
source_claim_supported: AAP recommends routine repeated postpartum depression screening with a validated tool at 1-, 2-, 4-, and 6-month well-child visits to identify parents who may need further evaluation, treatment, referral, and support for the parent-infant dyad.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance: provide preventive screening, health-promotion teaching, and age-appropriate family-centered care across pregnancy, postpartum, infancy, and childhood.
blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — postpartum depression screening during infant preventive care
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source rationale item into a realistic 2-month well-child scenario and anchored the exact 1-, 2-, 4-, and 6-month screening schedule directly to current AAP guidance. The final item distinguishes screening from diagnosis and tests why repeated pediatric screening remains appropriate rather than relying on vague claims that postpartum depression is merely 'common and underdiagnosed.'

audit_findings.clinical_category: postpartum depression screening / pediatric preventive care / parent-infant dyad
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified the exact well-child screening schedule and validated-tool requirement against AAP primary guidance and current AAP periodicity resources. The item does not depend on an unsupported prevalence estimate.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A reflects routine repeated screening and follow-up. B incorrectly converts a screening tool into a definitive diagnostic instrument. C improperly makes screening symptom-triggered. D contradicts AAP's repeated schedule through 6 months.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; it accurately states the preventive purpose and follow-up role of screening.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect but plausible screening-versus-diagnosis error; positive results require further evaluation.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; routine screening is recommended even without infant manifestations or an overt parental complaint.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; repeated screening at multiple early well-child visits is explicitly recommended.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A explains both why screening occurs in pediatric care and what should follow identification of risk. No other option is partially correct within the AAP schedule.
audit_findings.cueing: All four choices address the rationale or implications of screening at a well-child visit and are comparable in scope; no unrelated mental-health distractor is used.
audit_findings.blueprint: This is preventive screening and family-centered health promotion during infancy, fitting Health Promotion and Maintenance.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked whether the 2019 AAP schedule remains current; current AAP periodicity and implementation pages still list maternal depression screening at 1, 2, 4, and 6 months. Rechecked screening-versus-diagnosis wording and referral logic. No unsupported numeric precision or unresolved conflict remained.
